title: Laws of character
hookLine: diet, sleep, speech and health are spiritual practice

cards: Early in a book about knowing God, the subject changes. Suddenly there's advice about when to eat. Don't eat unless you're hungry.
Don't drink unless you're thirsty. Don't fill your stomach all the way; stop while there's still some room. Advice about sleep.
Advice about how much to talk. It sits in the Book of Knowledge, not far from the foundation of foundations, written in the same voice as the laws about God.

teach.b: De'ot. Usually translated character: the settled habits of a person's temper. Hilkhot De'ot, the laws of character.
Earlier this block we heard Maimonides on the middle way. Today he takes it into the body. First, the reason.

teach.h: A HEALTHY BODY CLEARS THE ROAD.
teach.b: Keeping the body healthy and whole, he says, is part of the ways of God, because a sick person can't understand or know the Creator. A body in pain pulls the mind away. Caring for it isn't vanity.
It's clearing the road. Second, the details. Eat when hungry.
Stop about a quarter short of full. Don't eat in a rush. Sleep enough, and at night.
He even writes about exercise before meals. A law code that reads, in places, like a doctor's note. Third, the intention.

teach.h: EAT, SLEEP, WORK FOR ONE AIM.
teach.b: A person should eat, drink, sleep and work with one aim, he says: a healthy body, so the soul can serve God.

Someone who lives that way serves God all the time, even while sleeping, because the rest is taken in order to serve. Sleep becomes a kind of worship, not for what happens during it, but for why. Fourth, speech.
Behind his advice sits the old teaching from Pirkei Avot: silence is a fence for wisdom. Diet, sleep, speech, health. Ordinary days, with a reason running underneath.

how: Some Jews study Hilkhot De'ot as practical guidance for daily habits, and Jews who keep the tradition say blessings before and after eating, turning ordinary meals into moments of attention.

o: a set of opinions a person argues for in debate
settled habits of character, the temper a person keeps
the debts a person owes to neighbors and friends

games.q: the laws of character — tap the pairs.
p: a sick person can't know the Creator
about a quarter short of full
sleep taken in order to serve

s: Maimonides treats health as a matter outside religion
he writes it into the Book of Knowledge: a healthy body is part of the ways of God.
he advises eating until completely full
he advises stopping about a quarter short of full.
he says even sleep can be service of God
if a person sleeps in order to have a healthy body for serving God, the sleep itself is service.

games.q: you're hungry, tired and busy. Maimonides is writing laws about knowing God. what does he say about your lunch and your sleep?
o: they don't matter; only the soul matters.
eat and sleep well, with the aim of a healthy body to serve God.
fast and stay awake as much as possible.
games.why: he says to eat, drink and sleep in measure, all aimed at health so the soul can serve. then even sleep becomes service.

practice: Notice, honestly, whether you're hungry right now, or just used to eating at this hour.

Then picture your next meal: sitting down, not rushing, tasting the first bite, pausing halfway to ask how full you are, stopping with a little room left. If you say a blessing before eating, imagine saying it slowly.

wordCard.voice: De'ot. Character, the settled habits of a person; and Hilkhot De'ot, Maimonides' laws of character, where eating, sleeping and speaking are done for the soul's sake. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: dispositions or character traits, the name of Hilkhot De'ot in the Book of Knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: the body serves the soul. Even sleep can be service, when you know why you rest. Until tomorrow.
